common_name: Minerva Rose of Sharon (Lavender-Pink Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Minerva is one of the original US National Arboretum rose of sharon introductions and remains one of the most widely available cultivars.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Minerva bears large, single to semi-double, lavender-pink flowers with a bold reddish-purple eye at the center, opening over a long season from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Like its sibling introductions Aphrodite and Diana, it is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection that sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older, seed-grown rose of sharon while remaining tough and heat-tolerant. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and maximize flowering wood.

common_name: Helene Rose of Sharon (White with Deep Red Veined Eye Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Helene is one of the original US National Arboretum rose of sharon introductions, prized for its crisp white-and-red flower contrast.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bred by the US National Arboretum, Helene bears crisp white, single flowers marked with a deep reddish-purple eye that radiates outward along the petal veins, a striking, high-contrast pattern distinct from the solid-eyed look of many other rose of sharon cultivars, blooming from midsummer into fall. Like its sibling introductions it is a sterile or nearly sterile triploid selection that sets little to no seed, avoiding the volunteer-seedling nuisance common with older, seed-grown rose of sharon while remaining a tough, heat- and humidity-tolerant shrub. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and maximize flowering wood.

common_name: Red Heart Rose of Sharon (Classic White with Red Center Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Heart is an older, long-cultivated rose of sharon and, unlike the sterile National Arboretum triploid introductions, can self-seed, so remove spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Red Heart is a classic, long-cultivated rose of sharon bearing large, single, pure white flowers with a bold crimson-red center, a simple but striking color combination that has kept it in continuous cultivation for generations. Blooming heavily from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub, it is tough, heat-tolerant, and easy to grow in average garden soil, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape and encourage the current season's flowering wood.

common_name: Bluebird Rose of Sharon (Clear Blue-Violet Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Bluebird is an older, long-cultivated rose of sharon and, unlike the sterile National Arboretum triploid introductions, can self-seed, so remove spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Bluebird is a widely grown, older rose of sharon selection carrying clear blue-violet, single flowers with a small red eye at the center, considered one of the truest blue tones available among rose of sharon cultivars, blooming heavily from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. It is tough and easy to grow in average garden soil, tolerating heat and humidity well, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern. It needs little care beyond an annual late-winter pruning to maintain shape.

common_name: Woodbridge Rose of Sharon (Classic Rosy-Pink Red-Eyed Althea)

planting.note: Set out container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Woodbridge is one of the most popular and widely available older rose of sharon cultivars, and unlike the sterile National Arboretum triploid introductions it can self-seed, so remove spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; prune in late winter to shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood. Woodbridge is one of the most popular and long-cultivated rose of sharon selections, bearing large, single, rich rosy-pink flowers with a deep red eye at the center, blooming prolifically from midsummer into fall on a vigorous, upright shrub. Its rich, saturated color and reliable heavy bloom have kept it a garden favorite for decades, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden soil with ease, though as an older, seed-fertile cultivar it can self-seed more readily than the sterile triploid selections bred more recently, so deadhead spent flowers if volunteer seedlings are a concern.
